origin_region: Southern Region · Shire Highlands (Thyolo and Mulanje)
cultivar: Assam-type seedling bushes and Malawian clones from the Tea Research Foundation of Central Africa (SFS and PC series)
processing: Mostly CTC for blends, fully oxidised and fired at estate factories; a few estates (Satemwa above all) run orthodox lines for leaf grades and hand-made speciality lots.
harvest_season: Mainly the rainy season from about November to April; plucking slows right down in the cool, dry months of the southern winter.
appearance_dry: Dark granules (CTC) or twisted dark leaf with some tips (orthodox).
taste_profile: Bright, brisk and clean with a touch of malt and a soft sweetness; the CTC is prized by blenders for colour, the orthodox lots show more honey and fruit.

brewing.notes: Just under the boil, 3–4 minutes, milk optional; leaf grades give a second steep.

vintage_note: Most of the crop is sold through the Limbe auction in Blantyre and in bulk to UK and South African blenders, so 'Malawi' rarely appears on a retail label; estate lots from Satemwa, Lujeri or the Eastern Produce gardens reach speciality shops by season and year. Buy the current season's lot and use within a year.
description:
Malawi is the oldest tea producer in Africa, with the first bushes planted in the late nineteenth century in the Shire Highlands of the south, around Thyolo and Mulanje, and it remains one of the continent's biggest growers. Most of its crop is CTC for British and South African blenders, but the region also has a few estates making orthodox and speciality teas, and Satemwa in Thyolo has done more than anyone to show what Malawian leaf can do.

Manufacture on the big estates is CTC, fully oxidised and fired at the factory; Satemwa and a couple of others run orthodox lines as well, rolling whole leaf for leaf grades and hand-making small lots. The crop comes mainly in the rainy season from about November to April, and the plucking slows right down in the cool, dry months of the southern winter.

The cup is bright reddish-copper, brisk and clean with a touch of malt and a soft sweetness; blenders prize the CTC for its colour, and the orthodox lots show more honey and fruit. Brew it with water just under the boil for three to four minutes, with or without milk, and expect a second steep from leaf grades.

Most of it is sold through the Limbe auction in Blantyre and in bulk to blenders, and 'Malawi' rarely appears on a retail label; estate lots from Satemwa, Lujeri or the Eastern Produce gardens reach speciality shops by season and year. Buy the current season's lot and use it within a year.

A good one to taste if you are curious what the 'other' African tea in your tea bag is.
sources_note: No Wikipedia article on Malawian tea, so 'Black tea' is used as umbrella ('Shire Highlands' and 'Thyolo District' exist but are not tea articles). Clone series names (SFS, PC) and the Limbe auction detail are from memory.
